rv.q: Waitress is a feel-good show that’s no mere guilty pleasure.
Even when the musical veers toward preciousness, Mueller’s performance grounds it in unimpeachable emotional authenticity.
Best of all, singer-songwriter Sara Bareilles, making her theatrical debut, supplies a set of songs that have her own distinctive twang of country-inflected pop yet also pulse with feeling.
Suddenly, a pleasant and polished but weightless musical comedy rises to transporting heights, and sweeps up your heart along with it.

Ms. Mueller’s vibrant performance of this gentle but wrenching song, featuring a melody that soars and then recedes in waves, is the high point of the show — and for that matter a high point of the Broadway season.
Mueller can really act as well as sing her heart out.
But the resulting musical, based on the quirky film Adrienne Shelly completed not long before her death, is both sweet and bitter and only sporadically satisfying.

Fresh and delicious, Waitress has an excellent ratio of sweet to tart; supporting characters who provide crustiness (Dakin Matthews's grumbly store owner) and flakiness (Christopher Fitzgerald's loony admirer of another waitress); and cooked-to-perfection staging by Diane Paulus.
What's most remarkable about Waitress is how it manages to be both deeply personal and broadly universal

"'Waitress' is a sweet slice of a show that shines with the help of a star ingredient: Tony winner Jessie Mueller...Bareilles has crafted an upbeat, tuneful score that sounds akin to the pop sounds she’s known for with layered harmonies and ballads alongside lively numbers...
Bareilles has created a cohesive, emotionally rich score that enhances rather than simply accompanies the storytelling.
The characters, broadened and amped up several notches to register on the large stage of a Broadway house, eventually do endear themselves even if they are just a bit shy of caricature.
Overall, this is a fairly auspicious debut
Nevertheless, mostly positive reviews may turn the show into the hit The Bridges of Madison County never was.
Even though it takes a lot to impress me when it comes to musicals, this one did.
A perfect blend of soulful music, funny dialogue and a quirky cast of characters forms the basis for quite an enjoyable evening in the theatre.
“It’s an audience-pleaser: a clever show with a soul...The music is buoyant, and the lyrics are thoughtful and honest, full of the humor and warmth that is infused throughout the show...

Bereft of any glamorous accoutrements, her work is especially vibrant, making transparent every turn in Jesse’s psyche, from her ethereal joy in simply massaging dough to the ambivalence about her pregnancy and the depths of her despair in her unhappiness with her marriage.
The show is only moderately entertaining, but apparently that’s enough to have kept it running this long.
But her performance in the very heavy book scenes is excellent, and she fights the inept writing of Jenna by always playing her for real.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this female-driven musical adaptation, praising Jessie Mueller's transcendent performance and Sara Bareilles' emotionally rich score, but faulting the broad, formulaic book that sweetens the film's intimate charm.
